question: What proportion of adults have a corrected serum calcium checked within 12 hours of thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy?
why: Post-operative hypocalcaemia is a common, preventable cause of delayed discharge and re-admission after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, and no closed-loop audit of the timing of the first postoperative calcium check has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Post-operative Hypocalcaemia Guidance
standard.wording: POST THYROIDECTOMY / PARATHYROIDECTOMY CORRECTED CALCIUM LEVELS: Check within 12h postoperatively

pass: Corrected serum calcium result is filed and actioned within 12 hours of the end of surgery
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing total or completion thyroidectomy, or parathyroidectomy. Exclusion: hemithyroidectomy or thyroid lobectomy only
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid or parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Theatre system for operation type and time, laboratory system for calcium sample time, EPR for the documented action
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 'post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery' order set that auto-requests a corrected calcium for 12 hours post-op and displays the BAETS treatment algorithm next to the result
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size, on the next 40 consecutive operations
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery/ENT MDT and departmental audit meeting; embed the order set as the default post-op set if the target is met
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library] related: NNA-069 (post-thyroidectomy observation schedule) shows the same order-set approach improving compliance with a post-thyroid surgery bundle
pitfalls: Sample drawn but result not checked out of hours → build the check into the nursing handover, not just the request
Small numbers at units doing few parathyroidectomies → combine thyroid and parathyroid cases for the denominator
Definition of 'checked' drifts between cycles (requested vs resulted) → fix the definition as 'result available in EPR' before cycle 1
New starters unaware of the algorithm → laminate the algorithm in recovery and on the ward
pearls: Recruit the endocrine surgery clinical nurse specialist to check for missed 12-hour bloods each morning
Agree the exact cut-off time (12h from skin closure, not from admission) before cycle 1 starts
Link the order set to the procedure code so it fires automatically
Keep the same nurse-led calcium round after the surgical trainees rotate
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from theatre system and EPR

question: What proportion of adults undergoing thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy have a documented post-operative laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord movement?
why: Vocal cord palsy is a leading cause of litigation after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, yet the true incidence is only known where laryngoscopy is performed routinely; no audit of compliance with mandatory post-operative laryngoscopy has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Post-operative laryngoscopy is required as a key quality control measure and should become mandatory.

pass: A fibreoptic or transcutaneous laryngoscopy assessment of vocal cord movement is documented at any point after surgery, up to and including the first outpatient follow-up
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing thyroid or parathyroid surgery. Exclusion: patients refusing the examination (documented separately)
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid/parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Operation note, ENT/voice clinic letters, EPR results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make a laryngoscopy booking (by the surgical team or ENT) a mandatory step on the electronic discharge checklist for every thyroid/parathyroid operation
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery MDT and joint ENT/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed the discharge checklist step if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: No ENT or voice clinic slots available → negotiate a ring-fenced weekly slot before cycle 1
Refusals not distinguished from omissions → add a separate 'declined' field so the denominator is fair
Surgeons doing their own transcutaneous ultrasound assessment not counted → agree what counts as 'laryngoscopy' before starting
Result not filed back into the surgical record → ask ENT to copy the surgical team into every report
pearls: Agree with ENT a same-day or next-day slot before starting the first cycle
Use a transcutaneous laryngeal ultrasound pathway where trained staff exist, to reduce reliance on ENT capacity
Put the laryngoscopy step on the WHO-style discharge checklist so it cannot be missed
Feed back cord palsy rates to the department each year so the mandatory step is not seen as a paperwork exercise
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR and clinic letters

question: What proportion of adults with a voice change or suspected/confirmed thyroid malignancy have a documented pre-operative laryngoscopy before thyroid or parathyroid surgery?
why: Pre-operative vocal cord assessment changes intraoperative and consent decisions when malignancy or voice change is present; no audit targeting this selective indication (rather than routine laryngoscopy in all patients) has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Pre-operative laryngoscopy in non-cancer patients with no history of voice change has a low rate of abnormal findings.

pass: A pre-operative laryngoscopy result is documented in the notes before surgery for any patient with a voice change or a cytological/clinical suspicion of malignancy
population: Inclusion: adults listed for thyroid or parathyroid surgery with documented voice change or suspected/confirmed malignancy. Exclusion: benign disease with a normal voice
sample: All patients with voice change or suspected malignancy listed for thyroid/parathyroid surgery over the last 6 months (expect 30-40)
data_source: Pre-assessment clinic letters, MDT proforma, ENT clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'voice change / suspected malignancy → pre-op laryngoscopy booked' field to the thyroid MDT outcome proforma
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the proforma field if it improves compliance
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Voice change not systematically asked about at clinic → add a standard voice question to the pre-assessment template
Small numbers if malignancy is rare locally → run over 6 months rather than 3
Laryngoscopy done but not documented in the surgical notes → require the ENT report to be filed in the same record
MDT proforma completed retrospectively → complete it in real time at the MDT
pearls: Add the voice question to every thyroid nodule clinic template, not just cancer clinics
Use the MDT coordinator to check the field is complete before the case is listed
Share abnormal pre-op findings with the operating surgeon before consent
Keep a log of pre-op abnormal cords to compare with post-op findings
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from MDT proforma

question: What proportion of adults with structural persistent thyroid cancer after total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine are discussed at the thyroid cancer multidisciplinary team meeting?
why: Persistent structural disease after primary treatment changes management (further surgery, radiotherapy or systemic treatment) and should not be managed outside the MDT; no audit of MDT discussion for this specific group has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.4 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss at the multidisciplinary team meeting any person who has had a total or completion thyroidectomy and RAI and has evidence of structural persistent disease.

pass: Documented discussion and outcome at the thyroid cancer MDT within 4 weeks of imaging or biochemistry showing structural persistent disease
population: Inclusion: adults with thyroid cancer who have had total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine and subsequent evidence of structural persistent disease. Exclusion: biochemical-only persistence with no structural correlate
sample: All such patients identified over the last 12 months (expect 20-30 in a regional cancer centre)
data_source: MDT database, oncology and endocrine clinic letters, imaging reports
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'structural persistent disease' MDT-list trigger from the radiology reporting system when a report contains that phrase for a coded thyroid cancer patient
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT and cancer services governance meeting; embed the radiology trigger if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Structural persistence identified in a non-cancer clinic and not flagged → educate all clinicians reviewing thyroid cancer follow-up scans
MDT list overloaded, cases delayed → create a fast-track 'persistent disease' slot
Ambiguity over what counts as 'structural' vs biochemical → agree the definition with radiology and oncology before cycle 1
Retrospective identification bias if reliant on memory → use a coded database search
pearls: Ask radiology to use a standard phrase ('structural persistent disease') in reports to enable searching
Give the MDT coordinator a standing search of the radiology system each week
Keep a register of persistent disease cases for continuity when staff rotate
Feed outcomes back to the referring endocrinologist so follow-up plans are updated
effort: ~30 min per month from MDT database and radiology search

question: What proportion of fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples for a thyroid nodule are reported as Thy1 (non-diagnostic/inadequate)?
why: A high non-diagnostic rate delays diagnosis and increases repeat procedures; no audit of local Thy1 rates against the NICE quality trigger has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.2.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider rapid on-site evaluation of FNAC adequacy rates to improve the diagnostic yield of samples if the Thy1 (inadequate) rate for the centre or individual healthcare professionals is higher than 15% (when Thy1c is excluded).

pass: Thy1 (excluding Thy1c) rate for the service is 15% or lower over the audit period
population: Inclusion: all thyroid nodule FNAC samples taken over the audit period. Exclusion: repeat FNAC on the same nodule within 4 weeks
sample: All thyroid FNAC samples over the last 6 months (expect 40-60)
data_source: Cytology reporting system, radiology (ultrasound-guided FNAC) records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) of FNAC adequacy for ultrasound-guided thyroid biopsies
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint cytology/radiology/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed ROSE if the target is met
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: ROSE requires a cytotechnologist or pathologist present at every list → negotiate cover before starting the change
Operator-level data seen as punitive → present anonymised operator codes first, agree feedback approach with the team
Thy1c cases wrongly counted as inadequate → use the coded cytology categories, not free text
Small numbers per individual operator → report at service level first, individual level only with consent
pearls: Agree with cytology in advance which category counts as 'inadequate' for the audit
Use a dedicated ultrasound-guided FNAC list run by trained operators to improve consistency
Share Thy1 rates quarterly at the endocrine surgery/radiology joint meeting
Track repeat-biopsy rate as a secondary outcome
effort: ~20 min per month from cytology reporting system

question: What proportion of patients with T1a/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without radioactive iodine receive the recommended surveillance ultrasound and annual clinical follow-up?
why: Under-surveillance risks missed recurrence in low-risk thyroid cancer managed without RAI; no audit of adherence to the NICE surveillance schedule has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.2 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider an ultrasound at 6 to 12 months initially then annual clinical follow-up for up to 5 years for people with T1a (m) or T1b stage or greater thyroid cancer, who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI.

pass: An ultrasound is booked or performed 6-12 months after surgery and an annual clinical follow-up appointment is booked for each year up to 5 years
population: Inclusion: adults with T1a(m)/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer treated by hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI. Exclusion: patients who received RAI
sample: All such patients treated in the last 18 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Cancer MDT database, radiology booking system, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'low-risk thyroid cancer surveillance' pathway on the cancer follow-up system that books the 6-12 month ultrasound and annual reviews at the point of MDT outcome
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the automated pathway if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from surgical clinic → use a single named follow-up pathway owner
Ultrasound slots not protected for surveillance → agree a standing allocation with radiology
Definition of T1a(m) vs T1a ambiguous to non-specialists → confirm staging with the MDT coordinator for each case
Surveillance stopped early without documented reason → require a reason field if follow-up is curtailed before 5 years
pearls: Use the MDT outcome form to auto-generate the follow-up schedule
Give patients a printed follow-up plan at their post-op clinic visit
Audit alongside the cancer MDT's annual outcomes review
Nominate a CNS to track the pathway centrally
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT database

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are not already taking a beta-blocker are offered pharmacological prophylaxis (amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) to reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation?
why: Postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery prolongs stay and increases stroke risk; while restarting a pre-existing beta-blocker is already tracked in the library [NNA-047], no audit has measured whether patients who are not already on a beta-blocker are offered any of the recommended prophylactic options.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.1 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery: reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation by offering 1 of the following: amiodarone a standard beta‑blocker (that is, a beta-blocker other than sotalol) a rate‑limiting calcium‑channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) do not offer digoxin.

pass: One of amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is prescribed for AF prophylaxis by the end of the first postoperative day, and digoxin is not used for this purpose
population: Inclusion: adults having elective cardiac surgery who were not on a beta-blocker before admission. Exclusion: patients on a pre-existing beta-blocker (covered by the restart pathway)
sample: 40 consecutive beta-blocker-naive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
data_source: Anaesthetic chart, ICU drug chart, EPMA
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'AF prophylaxis: amiodarone / beta-blocker / calcium-channel blocker (tick one) or contraindicated (reason)' line to the post-cardiac surgery ICU order set
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/anaesthesia governance meeting; embed the order set default if effective
evidence: [NNA-047] restarting a pre-existing beta-blocker by POD1 improved with a default ICU order-set line; the same approach is proposed here for beta-blocker-naive patients
pitfalls: Digoxin still used from habit → remove it as an option from the order set
Bradycardia or hypotension used as a blanket reason to omit prophylaxis without considering alternatives → require the alternative agent to be considered first
AF occurring after ICU discharge missed by the audit → extend data collection to hospital discharge
Anaesthetists and surgeons prescribing inconsistently → agree a single default order set for both teams
pearls: Build the three options into a single tick-box so an active choice is required
Involve pharmacy in checking interactions before amiodarone loading
Review the order set uptake weekly during the first cycle
Keep the postoperative AF rate as a linked outcome measure
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ICU drug chart

question: What proportion of patients started on a rhythm-control strategy for new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery have their need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment reassessed at around 6 weeks?
why: Postoperative AF often resolves once the precipitant settles, but antiarrhythmic drugs are frequently continued by default; no audit of the 6-week reassessment has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.6 (2021)
standard.wording: If a rhythm‑control strategy is chosen, reassess the need for antiarrhythmic drug treatment at a suitable time point (usually at around 6 weeks).

pass: A documented reassessment of the need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment occurs between 4 and 8 weeks after starting rhythm control
population: Inclusion: adults started on a rhythm-control strategy for new postoperative AF after cardiac surgery. Exclusion: rate-control strategy chosen
sample: All patients started on rhythm control for postoperative AF in the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Discharge summary, cardiology/cardiac surgery follow-up clinic letters, GP correspondence
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 6-week antiarrhythmic review task to the discharge summary for any patient discharged on antiarrhythmic treatment for postoperative AF
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery follow-up governance meeting; embed the discharge task if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Patients discharged to GP follow-up only, with no cardiology review booked → give GPs a clear stop/review date on the discharge letter
Reassessment done but not documented in a retrievable place → use a coded discharge summary field
Loss to follow-up if patients move between services → name a single team responsible for the review
Antiarrhythmics continued indefinitely 'to be safe' → present the evidence for time-limited use at teaching sessions
pearls: Give a clear stop/review date on every antiarrhythmic prescription at discharge
Use the cardiac surgery nurse specialist to track outstanding reviews
Feed reassessment outcomes back to the prescribing team
Align the review with an existing 6-week post-cardiac-surgery follow-up appointment where possible
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from discharge summaries

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are already taking a statin have it continued after surgery?
why: Unintentional omission of a pre-existing statin at the time of surgery is a recognised, avoidable medicines-reconciliation failure; no audit of statin continuation after cardiac surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.4 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery who are already on statins, continue this treatment.

pass: A pre-existing statin is represented on the post-operative drug chart by the end of the first postoperative day, or a documented reason for stopping it is recorded
population: Inclusion: adults on a statin before elective cardiac surgery. Exclusion: statin started for the first time postoperatively
sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients known to be on a statin pre-operatively, over the last 4 months
data_source: Medicines reconciliation record, ICU/ward drug chart

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add pre-existing statins to the medicines reconciliation prompt that appears automatically when writing the post-cardiac-surgery drug chart
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/pharmacy medicines safety meeting; embed the reconciliation prompt if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Statin omitted because the patient is nil by mouth and not represented once feeding resumes → add a re-check step once oral intake restarts
Reconciliation done by a junior doctor without pharmacy cross-check → involve pharmacy in every post-op reconciliation
Statin stopped for a genuine reason (e.g. rhabdomyolysis risk) but not documented → require a reason field
Discharge summary omits the statin even though it was continued in hospital → check the discharge letter as well as the inpatient chart
pearls: Use the electronic medicines reconciliation list as the single source of truth for pre-op medicines
Ask pharmacy to review post-cardiac-surgery drug charts within 24 hours
Flag any statin omission for consultant sign-off
Repeat the check at discharge as well as on the ward
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from drug charts

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery receive mechanical VTE prophylaxis from admission and, where indicated, pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days?
why: Cardiac surgery patients are at increased VTE risk from immobility and central access, but VTE prophylaxis is often deprioritised around anticoagulation for bypass; no audit of compliance with the NICE cardiac-surgery-specific VTE recommendations has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, recs 1.15.1 and 1.15.2 (2018)
standard.wording: 1.15.1 Consider mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery who are at increased risk of VTE. 1.15.2 Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery and are not having other anticoagulation therapy: Use LMWH as first-line treatment.

pass: Mechanical VTE prophylaxis is documented from admission, and pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH is prescribed for at least 7 days in patients not otherwise anticoagulated
population: Inclusion: adults undergoing cardiac surgery at increased VTE risk. Exclusion: patients already anticoagulated for another indication
sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
data_source: VTE risk assessment form, drug chart, nursing records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a cardiac-surgery-specific VTE prophylaxis bundle (mechanical from admission plus a 7-day LMWH course) to the admission and post-op order sets
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery governance meeting; embed the bundle if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Mechanical prophylaxis omitted because of leg swelling or drains → give clear guidance on device choice around chest drains and vein harvest sites
LMWH delayed because of concern about bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass → agree a standard start day with the surgical team before cycle 1
7-day course not completed because of early discharge → include a discharge prescription for the remaining days
VTE risk assessment completed but not linked to a prescribing action → link the assessment directly to the order set
pearls: Build both mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis into a single order-set bundle
Agree the LMWH start time with cardiac surgery and anaesthesia in advance
Audit alongside existing VTE risk-assessment compliance data
Keep a discharge checklist item for completing the 7-day course
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from drug chart and VTE assessment

question: What proportion of adults with an undiagnosed or symptomatic pleural effusion who need a pleural procedure have it within 5 days of the decision being made?
why: Delays to pleural drainage prolong breathlessness and hospital stay; no audit of time from decision to pleural procedure against the national access standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, quality statement on access to pleural services
standard.wording: For symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion, where a pleural procedure is clinically indicated, it should be offered within five days of the decision being made, unless the patient's symptoms or evidence of infection makes a more urgent procedure necessary.

pass: The pleural procedure is performed within 5 calendar days of the documented decision to proceed, or sooner if urgent
population: Inclusion: adults with a symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion referred to the cardiothoracic/pleural service for a procedure. Exclusion: emergency drainage for tension physiology or empyema requiring immediate intervention
sample: 40 consecutive referrals for pleural procedures over the last 3 months
data_source: Referral log, procedure booking system, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up a weekly protected pleural procedure list with direct electronic referral from the point of decision
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the pleural service/cardiothoracic MDT; embed the protected list if effective
evidence: [NNA-398], [NNA-399], [NNA-400], [NNA-401] audit thoracic ultrasound use, the pleural safety checklist, effusion sampling in pneumonia and referral for recurrent pneumothorax; this audit adds the time from decision to procedure, which none of those measure
pitfalls: 'Decision made' not consistently documented, making the start point unclear → agree a single documentation point (referral form date) before cycle 1
Procedure delayed by lack of ultrasound-trained operators → identify capacity gaps early
Urgent cases wrongly counted against the 5-day target → add an explicit urgent-indication field
Referrals lost between teams → use a single electronic referral pathway
pearls: Use a single electronic referral form that timestamps the decision
Protect a weekly list specifically for non-urgent pleural procedures
Involve the pleural nurse specialist in tracking waiting referrals
Review the waiting list weekly at the pleural MDT
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from referral log

question: What proportion of patients are given information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact, documented before discharge after cardiac surgery?
why: Sternal wound infection after cardiac surgery is a high-harm complication, and early patient recognition and re-presentation depend on clear safety-netting advice; no audit of documented SSI safety-netting specifically after cardiac surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG125 Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment, rec 1.1.3 (2019)
standard.wording: Offer patients and carers information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact if they are concerned.

pass: The discharge summary or a discrete leaflet documents that wound infection safety-netting advice (signs to watch for and a contact number) was given
population: Inclusion: all adults discharged after cardiac surgery via median sternotomy. Exclusion: patients who die before discharge
sample: 40 consecutive cardiac surgery discharges over the last 3 months
data_source: Discharge summary, nursing discharge checklist

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'sternal wound infection advice and contact number given' tick box to the cardiac surgery discharge summary template, linked to a standard leaflet
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery governance and infection prevention meeting; embed the discharge tick box if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Advice given verbally but not documented → make documentation itself, not just the conversation, the pass criterion
Leaflet given but generic (not sternal-wound specific) → develop a cardiac-surgery-specific leaflet
Patients discharged out of hours without the usual checklist → audit weekend/evening discharges separately
Field ticked as a default without the conversation happening → spot-check with post-discharge phone calls
pearls: Make the leaflet part of the standard cardiac surgery discharge pack
Give the same information to family/carers where the patient has reduced capacity
Include the sternal wound infection bundle as an agenda item at governance meetings
Track re-presentation rates for wound infection as a linked outcome
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from discharge summaries

question: What proportion of children undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion reach theatre within 3 hours of the decision to operate?
why: Testicular salvage falls sharply with delay to surgery; no closed-loop audit of time from decision to operate to incision for suspected torsion has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion
standard.wording: Timely intervention: Percentage of explorations within 3 hours of decision to operate (NCEPOD 2) (excluding those with co-morbidities) 100%

pass: Time from documented decision to operate to skin incision is 3 hours or less
population: Inclusion: all children undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion. Exclusion: children with significant co-morbidities delaying anaesthesia
sample: All scrotal explorations for suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 20-40)
data_source: Theatre system, emergency department and surgical clerking notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a 'suspected testicular torsion' theatre booking category that bypasses the routine emergency list queue and alerts theatre coordination directly
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery/emergency theatre governance meeting; embed the booking category if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Decision-to-operate time not documented consistently → agree a single trigger point (consultant/registrar decision documented in notes) before cycle 1
Theatre unavailable out of hours → confirm the emergency theatre escalation pathway covers torsion explicitly
Low case numbers per quarter → collect over 12 months to get a meaningful sample
Fasting status used to justify delay despite clinical urgency → reiterate that assessment should not be delayed by fasting status
pearls: Agree the torsion pathway with emergency medicine, theatres and anaesthesia before starting
Use a single-page torsion pathway sheet that timestamps each step
Review every case with a time over 3 hours at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Track testicular salvage rate as the outcome that matters to families
effort: ~15 min per case from theatre and ED records

question: What proportion of children presenting to a secondary care hospital with suspected testicular torsion are explored locally rather than transferred to a tertiary paediatric surgery centre?
why: Transfer delays testicular salvage and should be exceptional; no audit of unnecessary inter-hospital transfer for suspected torsion has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion
standard.wording: Transfer of a boy with a suspicion of torsion from a Secondary Care Institution to a Tertiary Care Centre should therefore be an exceptional occurrence (e.g. medical comorbidities).

pass: The child is explored at the presenting secondary care hospital unless a documented medical co-morbidity or other exceptional reason requires transfer
population: Inclusion: children presenting to a secondary care hospital with suspected testicular torsion. Exclusion: children presenting directly to a tertiary centre
sample: All secondary care presentations with suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
data_source: Emergency department notes, transfer records, theatre system
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree and circulate a local on-call rota and skills sign-off so that a competent surgeon and anaesthetist are always available locally for suspected torsion, with transfer requiring consultant-to-consultant agreement
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery network governance meeting; embed the local competency rota if effective
evidence: [no directly comparable closed-loop audit in the library]
pitfalls: Transfer driven by lack of confidence rather than genuine need → provide simulation training for on-call teams
Reasons for transfer not documented → make a reason field mandatory in the transfer request
Network guidance not known to on-call staff → include the pathway in induction
Transfer perceived as 'safer' despite adding delay → present time-to-theatre and salvage outcome data alongside transfer rates
pearls: Use network-level data sharing so all sites can benchmark

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg (or 130/80 mmHg if significant proteinuria) recorded at their most recent follow-up visit?
